flows.notes: Every claim here is read off the program's own report against a SUPPLIED project, never off code the scenario wrote. flows.title: Open the dashboard and find your way around
flows.goal: A developer starts the dashboard in a repository, lands on that repository's page, and learns where everything is.
flows.notes:
The dashboard area's front door, and the flow every other dashboard flow's arrival step assumes. It walks one journey in the order the Overview page itself narrates it: the command starts a server on a known port, asks the first-run mode question, holds the terminal in console mode, opens a browser, and lands on the page for the repository you are standing in — including the "standing in" rule, which is only falsifiable when the command runs from a NESTED subdirectory, so the seed carries one. Registration is proved as an effect of that first open (the repository was not registered before), and the CLI-wrote-it/dashboard-reads-it claim is proved off the arranging `truecourse analyze --no-llm`: the page shows a run the dashboard never executed. The rest of the walk is orientation — header identity, the left rail, the Home split, the section dropdown and what each section covers, the URL that carries section+tab, Back/Forward over those views, and the theme toggle that survives a reload.

CONFIGURATION SPLIT: this is the CONSOLE path of the mode choice; `run-the-dashboard-as-a-background-service` is its `variant` sibling and owns every service-mode claim of the same section.

Deliberately left for a later batch, from sections this flow binds: `--console` skips the mode prompt (mutually exclusive with the first-run prompt milestone inside ONE sandbox — the flag claim needs a home with NO saved mode, and answering the first-run prompt saves one; it belongs with a mode-prompt-focused flow that starts from a second fresh home); `PORT` moves the server (its own configuration variant); the whole repository-list surface (paste-a-path, Browse, the trash icon and its three consequences) which is a repository-management journey, not an orientation one; the sidebar-drag claim (drag interaction, batched with the Files/Flows/Databases walk); and the `?file=`/`?flow=`/`?view=diff` URL claims, which are proved where those surfaces are opened (flows 9 and 10).

REALIZATION RISKS: the first-run mode question is a TTY prompt, so the arranging command needs a scripted-stdin step (scenario format v3 `tty: true`), not a plain exec; `--console` holds the terminal, so the step that starts it can never be a blocking foreground run the scenario waits on; browser Back/Forward needs history control the web driver may not expose; and the theme-persistence milestone needs the SAME browser profile across a reload (a fresh context would lose the stored choice and fail the claim for the wrong reason).

flows.title: Run the dashboard as a background service
flows.goal: A developer runs the dashboard as a background service and manages it from the shell: status, logs, re-prompt, stop and uninstall.
flows.notes:
The SERVICE path of the console-vs-service configuration choice, so it is a `variant` of `open-the-dashboard-and-find-your-way-around` and never repeats its orientation walk: everything past the landing page belongs to the sibling flow. It carries exactly the lifecycle the Overview page's command block promises, in lifecycle order — `--service` skips the mode question (falsifiable only from a home with no saved mode, which is why this flow starts from its own fresh one), returns the shell with the dashboard serving, opens the browser at the same repository page the console mode does, survives the starting terminal closing, then `status`, `logs`, `--reconfigure`, `stop` and `uninstall`.

The either-mode milestone is the one claim in this section that spans BOTH configuration paths ("whichever mode you pick"): it is proved here rather than in the console flow because this is where the second mode exists, and its console half is settled by the sibling flow's landing milestone. `--reconfigure` sits after the service is up on purpose — re-asking is only meaningful once a mode has been saved, which the `--service` run did.

Deliberately left for a later batch: `PORT`, and the console flag claims (see the sibling flow's note on why the flag and the first-run prompt cannot be proved in one sandbox).

REALIZATION RISKS: the whole flow depends on a supplied host capability — installing a user service, keeping it alive across the starting shell's exit, and tailing its log — none of which a hermetic sandbox can fabricate; if the runner cannot bind it, this flow blocks alone while its console sibling still runs (which is the point of splitting them). `logs` is doubly conditional: the claim itself says logs exist in service mode ONLY, so the negative half (console mode reporting logs unavailable) cannot be shown here and stays with the console-mode batch. `uninstall` must be the last step — every earlier milestone needs the service installed.

The empty-state edge: everything the dashboard shows before a repository has any analysis data. flows.title: Run an analysis from the dashboard
flows.goal: A developer presses Analyze in the dashboard, answers the dirty-tree and LLM gates, and watches the run to completion.
flows.notes:
One press of Analyze, followed all the way through both gates and the whole in-flight surface. The order is the doc's own and is load-bearing: the dirty-tree dialog must be shown to come FIRST and the LLM confirm only after it, which is why the seed dirties the tree AND enables LLM rules — with either condition missing the ordering claim is unfalsifiable. The walk answers the stash dialog with "Don't stash" (so the uncommitted edit is what gets analyzed and the choice is observable in the findings), accepts the LLM gate, then reads the progress card: it exists at the bottom, ticks steps off, details the active one, and survives a tab switch. Completion is proved three ways — every view refreshes without a reload, the findings match what the CLI records for the same commit, and `.truecourse/logs/analyze.log` grew — and the flow closes on the transport claims, which are about this very run (it used the saved transport) and about what it must NOT have done (touched the credential file).

Deliberately left for a later batch, from sections this flow binds: the OTHER answer to each gate (Stash and analyze committed state; Skip — deterministic rules only) and every way of dismissing the dirty-tree dialog (X, backdrop, Escape) — alternative-answer paths that each need their own run and read as their own flows; the four conditions that SKIP the stash prompt (clean tree, subdirectory of a larger repo, git unavailable, `.truecourse/`-only changes), which are four different starting worlds; the three config-honoring claims (categories, LLM toggle, disabled rules), which want a config-driven flow; the estimate-matches-the-CLI cross-check; Cancel and the failed-run card (an error-path edge flow); and the CLI pre-answer flags in the page's closing Tip.

REALIZATION RISKS: this is the one dashboard flow that spends money — accepting the LLM gate means a real model call, so it needs the supplied transport and will block without it. "Runs in the dashboard server's own process" is asserted negatively (no separate analyze process exists while the run is in flight), which needs host process observation the web driver alone cannot do — a mixed step. The progress-card milestones are all races against a short run: on a seed small enough to analyze in a second, the card may never be observed, so the seeded project must be large enough for the run to stay in flight across the tab switch.

flows.title: Read a violation card and silence its rule
flows.goal: A developer reads a finding on its card, silences the rule that raised it, and turns it back on from the Rules panel.
flows.notes:
One card, read and then acted on. The first half stays on a single violation card — its two badges, its title and description, its file and line, the fix prompt it expands and the same text landing on the clipboard — and the second half follows the rule that raised it out of the list and back in: the ⋮ menu names the rule key it will disable, choosing it drops those findings from the list and from the analytics numbers at once, the key appears in `<repo>/.truecourse/config.json`, `truecourse rules list` agrees, and the stored analysis still contains the hidden findings (the claim that makes the whole thing reversible). The return path goes through the Rules panel deliberately: the shield opens it, the panel's rule count is cross-checked against the CLI, the All/On/Off switch and its disabled count are the natural way to FIND the rule that was just silenced, and flipping its switch proves both the per-repository toggle and the straight-away refresh — which is also the observation for re-enabling restoring the findings with nothing re-run.

Deliberately left for a later batch, from sections this flow binds: backticked identifiers rendering as code and the architecture card's `service / module / function` target (both need a finding with specific content — a later card-rendering batch); Open and Locate, which are entries into other surfaces and are proved where they land (the files walk and the graph walk); "skipped on future analyses" and "costs nothing to run", which need a second analysis run and an LLM rule; the resolved-findings-cannot-be-silenced claim, which needs diff mode; and the Rules panel's own catalogue surface (its search/severity/Det-LLM controls, its category tabs, the rule row's five metadata fields, the per-language badges and their hover text, and the switch writing to `disabledRules`) — a browse-the-catalogue journey rather than this silence-and-restore one.

REALIZATION RISKS: Copy Fix requires reading the system clipboard, which a headless web driver may not be permitted to do (a likely coverage gap, and the reason the fix-prompt EXPANSION milestone precedes it — the expanded text is the comparison target). The ⋮ menu is an icon-only control, so it needs a locator the current client actually exposes. Doc-drift watch, inherited from the analyze area's dashboard flow: the docs put the Rules panel behind a shield at the right of the filter row, while the client has been seen rendering a "Browse Rules" control — the milestone stays authored to the doc so a run surfaces the drift instead of hiding it. flows.title: Explore the architecture graph
flows.goal: A developer opens the architecture graph, sets its depth and canvas options, and clicks around the detected system.
flows.notes:
The graph as a reading surface: what it draws, at which depth, with which canvas options, and what a click does. Depth is walked in the order the page lists it — Services first (where the whole system is visible and hovering is meaningful), then the two scoped depths, which are reached through the empty-scope card and the selector the page says appears beside the toggle. The canvas toggles are read as a block, closing on the claim that binds them together (they live in the browser, not in the repo), which is also the only one of them with a disk-side assertion.

A DELIBERATE CONTRADICTION IS COMPOSED HERE, and it is the flow's most valuable step. The `Clicking around` section says both that clicking a service, module, function or DATABASE node zooms to it (milestone 12) and that clicking a database node switches to the Databases tab and opens that database's schema (milestone 19). The two outcomes cannot both follow one click on one node. Per the corpus rule the docs are not pre-fixed to help a flow: both claims are carried, in the order the page states them, and at most one of them can pass. Whichever fails is the deliverable — doc drift if the UI has one settled behaviour, a product bug if the UI does something else again. The zoom milestone is worded over four node kinds, so the scenario should exercise it on a SERVICE node and let the database click stand alone as the contradicting step; that keeps the failure attributable to the database sentence rather than to the general one.

Deliberately left for a later batch: the whole `Arranging it` section (dragging nodes, per-branch/per-depth persistence, surviving reload and re-analysis, Auto layout discarding positions, collapse/expand and its saved state, `ui-state.json` and its gitignore status) — a layout-persistence journey that needs reloads, a branch switch and a second analysis, and reads as its own flow; `Arriving from elsewhere` (Locate from a violation card, its depth switch, the Files crosshair and clearing the focus), which is an entry-point journey shared with the violations and files pages; the single-candidate auto-selection; the minimap and the move/select mode toggle; and the Live/Offline pill with its stalled-progress consequence, which needs the event stream cut mid-run.

REALIZATION RISKS: hover (milestone 7) and the three edge/animation toggles assert visual treatments — dimmed edges, curved versus L-shaped paths, motion — that need computed-style or geometry reads rather than text, and the animation claim may have no honest observation at all in a driver that cannot see motion. The canvas is a React Flow surface whose nodes have historically had no role or accessible name (recorded as transform gap G76 by the analyze area's dashboard flow), so every locator here is at risk; if the driver cannot address nodes, this flow blocks as a whole rather than degrading into fake passes. REALIZATION FEEDBACK (scenario batch): the supplied analysis-target binding proved unnecessary — every requirement here is met by a deterministic seeded project the scenario arranges and analyzes itself, which is what makes the content-exact assertions falsifiable; moved to seedable.
